paras: The attempted lynching of Ira Waters took place at Spartanburg, South Carolina, on July 30, 1888, when a party of white men came to take Waters, a Black prisoner, from the jail and lynch him. A deputy sheriff secretly removed him and delivered him to Columbia for safe keeping. Papers told the story chiefly as an account of the deputy's escape with his prisoner.

About a week earlier, Waters had been arrested and jailed at Spartanburg, charged with attempting a criminal assault on a white woman sixteen miles north of the town. It was "claimed," the Savannah Morning News said, that the approach of some white men had stopped him.

According to the Savannah account, Sheriff Gentry of Spartanburg learned two days before the removal that men from the neighborhood of the alleged crime had threatened to take the prisoner from the jail. Early on Monday morning a party of such men came into Spartanburg, where they were understood to be "only awaiting reinforcements before attacking the jail." The sheriff then told his son, Deputy Sheriff J. J. Gentry, to get the prisoner out of the city as secretly as possible.

The deputy took Waters out through the rear entrance of the jail and into the countryside. A Columbia dispatch said they took to the woods and caught a train for Greenwood, where Waters was chained in a room overnight; the Savannah account said they walked about fifteen miles to a train on the Laurens road. They reached Columbia on Tuesday, July 31, "much used up," with Waters still handcuffed and the key lost.
The coverage does not report any arrests of the party, a trial of Waters, or what became of him after he reached Columbia.

The Newberry Herald and News printed the Columbia dispatch on August 2 as "Smuggled from Spartanburg," with the deck "A Negro Prisoner who Barely Escaped Lynching," and closed on the lost handcuff key. The Savannah Morning News ran a longer, separately written version on August 6 among other South Carolina items, calling the case an "alleged crime" and describing the party without comment.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Ira Waters
bases: A party of white men came to Spartanburg to take Waters from the jail and lynch him, and he was removed before they acted (A2, A3).

Waters was not killed; the deputy sheriff removed him from the Spartanburg jail and delivered him to Columbia (A2, A3). The episode was a threatened lynching by a party of unstated size acting on an accusation of attempted assault on a white woman (A2, A3).

Two differently worded accounts, a Columbia dispatch in the Newberry paper and a longer item in the Savannah Morning News, agree on the charge, the lynching party and the removal to Columbia (A2, A3).

accounts.gist: A party of white men came to Spartanburg to lynch Waters; the deputy smuggled him to the woods, then by train to Greenwood, where he was chained in a room overnight, and on to Columbia.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News South Carolina column
accounts.gist: After reports of lynching threats, men from the crime's neighborhood came into Spartanburg early Monday and awaited reinforcements; the deputy took Waters out the rear of the jail, walked about fifteen miles and boarded a train on the Laurens road.

framing.detail: Headlined 'SMUGGLED FROM SPARTANBURG' with the deck 'A Negro Prisoner who Barely Escaped Lynching', the dispatch dwells on the deputy's flight and ends with the lost handcuff key.
A news-column item that reports the accusation as a 'charge' and an 'alleged crime' and describes the lynching party without comment.
